name: The Lost Dog Poster
blurb: A lost-dog poster keeps following a lonely newcomer, until it turns up on their own door
title: The Lost Dog Poster: 60-Second Twist Script for 2
description: A 60-second vertical twist script for 2: a lonely newcomer keeps finding the same lost-dog poster, then calls the number. Wholesome, free to film.
h1: The Lost Dog Poster: a 60-Second Wholesome Twist Script for 2 People
logline: Someone new to the neighbourhood keeps passing the same lost-dog poster, on a lamp post, at the bus stop, and then taped to their own front door. Unsettled, they finally call the number. The dog is not the one who is lost.
setting: A street, a bus stop, a front door and a park bench. Props: a printed lost-dog poster with a photo, tape, two phones, a calm dog on a lead or a dog toy.

roles.name: Ren
roles.note: 20s, any gender, recently moved to the city, polite, quietly lonely.

roles.name: Mr. Hale
roles.note: 65 to 80, any gender if renamed, kind, a little shy, walks the dog every day.

script.action: REN walks past a lamp post with earbuds in. A poster: LOST DOG. A scruffy dog photo. A phone number.
The same poster, at the bus stop. Ren slows down.
The same poster, taped to Ren's own front door.

script.say: Hi. I keep finding your poster. Everywhere. Is Biscuit still lost?

script.action: MR. HALE sits on a bench. A happy dog sits at his feet on a lead.

script.say: Never was. I moved here in spring. Nobody knocks. So I put up posters, people call, we talk a minute.
I see you walk past every day. Headphones in. Eyes down. You looked lost.

script.action: Ren sits down next to him. The dog puts its head on Ren's knee.

script.say: Nine days. You're the first person I've talked to.

script.action: Mr. Hale holds out the lead.

script.say: Six o'clock tomorrow. He walks better with two.

Day 9 caption, poster on Ren's door: that's personal

body: Shoot vertical 9:16 and film the three poster days on three different days if you can, in the same clothes, so the light changes and time feels real. Morning or late afternoon light makes the park scene glow. Record the phone call twice, once on Ren's side and once on Mr. Hale's, then cut between them. For the bench, put the phone on a small tripod at chest height and run the whole scene three or four times, keeping the take with the longest natural pause.

ul: Ren starts curious, then a little uneasy at the door. Play it as mild confusion, not fear, so the story stays warm.
Mr. Hale's question, where are you, should sound like a careful hope, not a mystery. He has waited a long time for a call.
The posters speech is a confession. Mr. Hale looks at the dog, not at Ren, until the line about the door.
Ren's nine days line is the real twist. Say it to the dog, quietly, and do not cry. Holding it back is stronger.
If you use a real dog, keep it on a lead and calm, and let the owner stand just out of frame. A toy dog in a basket works too.
Swap the dog for a lost cat or a lost parrot poster, and set the meeting at a balcony or a corner shop instead of a park.
Make Ren a retired person new to the area and Mr. Hale a student far from home, so the loneliness runs the other way.
Part-two hook: the next morning there is a new poster on Mr. Hale's door, put up by Ren, inviting the whole street for a walk.

faq.q: Do I need a real dog?
faq.a: No. A calm borrowed dog is lovely, but a soft toy dog in a basket or a dog only heard off screen also works. Never stress an animal for a take; keep it on a lead with its owner nearby.

faq.q: Can I use this script in a school film competition?
faq.a: Yes. It is free under CC BY 4.0 for competitions, classes and monetised channels. Credit "Script: cv.cm" in the end card or the description.

faq.q: How do I make the poster?
faq.a: Print or hand draw a simple sheet with LOST DOG, a photo of the dog you use, a name and a fake number. Avoid putting a real phone number on it, since people may call.
